Bun runtime fetched from github.com/oven-sh/bun during npm install (Bitwarden CLI hijack) AIDelivery High
Detects the @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 preinstall loader (bw_setup.js) downloading the Bun JavaScript runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases at npm install time. Legitimate Bitwarden CLI installs perform zero network activity, so a node child spawned by npm pulling the bun-v1.3.13 zip is a high-fidelity supply-chain signal. Rationale: Anchors on the exact loader filename `bw_setup.js`, the Bun release URL path `github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases`, and the specific `bun-v1.3.13` version named in the article — combined with the `npm/yarn/pnpm -> node` install-time parent chain that legitimate Bitwarden CLI installs never produced (article: "every prior release had no install lifecycle scripts"). Cross-checked StepSecurity post and oven-sh/bun release URL pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/bitwarden-cli-hijacked-on-npm-bun-staged-credential-stealer-targets-developers-github-actions-and-ai-tools • https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately scripting Bun installation in a Dockerfile or postinstall (will still alert; review parent package)
  • CI bootstrap scripts that pull Bun for benchmark or test purposes
  • Internal developer tooling that wraps the official Bun installer
  • Mirror proxies rewriting github.com URLs in corporate environments
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--save-dev bun","npm install -g bun")) | where not(DeviceName startswith "BUILD-")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 (or any version after 2026.3.0 with a preinstall hook) in the npm/yarn/pnpm install log on the host; pull the SHA256 of bw_setup.js and bw1.js from %APPDATA%\npm-cache or node_modules and compare to article hashes. 2) Contain: isolate the developer host, revoke that user's GitHub/npm/AWS/GCP tokens and any SSH keys present in ~/.ssh, force-rotate Bitwarden master password and 2FA. 3) Hunt: across the org search for the bw_setup.js / bw1.js hashes, any host that reached audit.checkmarx.cx or 94.154.172.43, and any workflow_run/workflow_dispatch events GitHub-side originating from compromised PATs in the last 30d.

| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;
let Preinstall = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bw_setup.js","@bitwarden/cli")
   or (FileName =~ "node.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm-cli.js","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "preinstall")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
BunDownload
| join kind=inner Preinstall on DeviceId
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, Timestamp1)) <= 120
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=tostring(AccountName), InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, PreinstallCmd=ProcessCommandLine

| where abs(datetime_diff('second', NetTime, ProcTime)) <= 120

TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli stealer exfil to audit.checkmarx.cx (94.154.172.43) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound traffic to the Checkmarx-impersonating exfil domain audit.checkmarx.cx (resolving 94.154.172.43) used by the bw1.js stealer. The legitimate Checkmarx parent domain is checkmarx.com — any host or process reaching audit.checkmarx.cx is article-specific stealer C2. Rationale: Both the domain `audit.checkmarx.cx` and IP `94.154.172.43` are named explicitly in the article and pre-extracted as IOCs. The `.cx` TLD impersonation of Checkmarx (real domain `checkmarx.com`) means any traffic to this domain is by definition unauthorised. Cross-checked StepSecurity disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/bitwarden-cli-hijacked-on-npm-bun-staged-credential-stealer-targets-developers-github-actions-and-ai-tools

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally visiting the lookalike domain for IOC validation (whitelist the analyst workstation)
  • Threat-intel feed scrapers / sandbox VMs detonating samples
  • Internal DNS sinkhole forwarding the query for telemetry
  • Proxy categorisation services performing on-demand reputation lookups
Suppression filter
| where not(Proc in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and Cmd has_any ("--incognito","sandbox-detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process making the connection — bw1.js typically runs under `bun.exe` or `node.exe` with bw1.js in the command line; correlate with @bitwarden/cli presence in node_modules. 2) Contain: block audit.checkmarx.cx and 94.154.172.43 at the egress firewall and DNS RPZ; isolate any host that hit either; treat all secrets that ever lived on the host (SSH keys, ~/.npmrc tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/GCP creds, ~/.claude.json) as compromised and rotate. 3) Hunt: pivot on Bun process spawns with no business need org-wide, and review any GitHub workflow_dispatch / workflow file additions in repos owned by affected users in the last 30 days.

| order by Timestamp desc

Known-malicious bw_setup.js / bw1.js SHA256 dropped under @bitwarden/cli AIInstallation High
Hash-based detection for the two stealer artefacts shipped inside @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 — bw_setup.js (loader) and bw1.js (9.7 MB obfuscated payload). Either hash on disk under a node_modules/@bitwarden/cli path is a guaranteed-true-positive indicator of the supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Both SHA-256 hashes (bw_setup.js, bw1.js) are explicitly published in the article body with file labels and pre-extracted in the IOC block. Filename + node_modules\@bitwarden\cli path gives a second-axis fallback if the attacker recompresses the tarball and the hash drifts. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/bitwarden-cli-hijacked-on-npm-bun-staged-credential-stealer-targets-developers-github-actions-and-ai-tools
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst extracting the samples in a sandbox VM that ships telemetry to production SIEM
  • IOC researcher carrying the hash list in a notes/markdown file that AV scans
  • Backup/restore operations replaying historical filesystem state from an already-infected host
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\","\\malware-samples\\","\\quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path is under node_modules\@bitwarden\cli and the host installed @bitwarden/cli at or after the publish timestamp of 2026.4.0; capture npm-shrinkwrap/package-lock and ~/.npm/_logs for the install trace. 2) Contain: kill any running bun.exe / node.exe processes referencing bw1.js, isolate the host, force-revoke npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/GCP keys, SSH keys, and the user's Bitwarden vault credentials (master password + 2FA reset). 3) Hunt: pivot to other hosts that pulled @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 (search package-lock changes in repos), and search GitHub audit logs for new workflow files created in repos owned by the user(s) in the last 30 days — the malware injects malicious workflows when it finds a GitHub token.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb","8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where SHA256 in (BadHashes) or (FileName in~ ("bw_setup.js","bw1.js") and FolderPath has "@bitwarden\\cli")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, User=InitiatingProcessAccountName),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where SHA256 in (BadHashes) or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bw_setup.js","bw1.js")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, User=AccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadHashes = dynamic(["18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb","8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where SHA256 in (BadHashes) or (FileName in~ ("bw_setup.js","bw1.js") and FolderPath has "@bitwarden\\cli")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, User=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="DeviceFileEvents"),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where SHA256 in (BadHashes) or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bw_setup.js","bw1.js")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, User=AccountName, Source="DeviceProcessEvents"),
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where TargetFileSHA256 in (BadHashes) or TargetFileName in~ ("bw_setup.js","bw1.js")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActionType=EventType, FileName=TargetFileName, FolderPath=TargetFilePath, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256, Initiator=ActingProcessName, InitiatorCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine, User=ActorUsername, Source="ImFileEvent"),
  (SecurityEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) and EventID == 4688
   | where CommandLine has_any ("bw_setup.js","bw1.js") or FileHash in (BadHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, ActionType="4688", FileName=NewProcessName, FolderPath=tostring(""), SHA256=FileHash, Initiator=ParentProcessName, InitiatorCmd=CommandLine, User=SubjectUserName, Source="SecurityEvent")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious Bitwarden CLI Stealer Artefact (bw_setup.js / bw1.js)
id: 7e4d1a3c-2c9b-4d7e-9f1a-8e3c5d0b2f44
description: Detects creation or execution of the bw_setup.js loader or bw1.js 9.7 MB obfuscated stealer payload from the @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 supply-chain compromise, matched by SHA256 or by name when located under an @bitwarden/cli node_modules path.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/bitwarden-cli-hijacked-on-npm-bun-staged-credential-stealer-targets-developers-github-actions-and-ai-tools
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1027
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_hash:
    Hashes|contains:
      - '18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb'
      - '8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14'
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\bw_setup.js'
      - '\bw1.js'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\@bitwarden\cli\'
  condition: selection_hash or selection_name
falsepositives:
  - None — both filenames are unique to the malicious release; legitimate @bitwarden/cli has no preinstall artefacts
level: critical
(@file.hash.sha256:(18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb OR 8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14) OR @Hashes:(*18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb* OR *8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14*) OR @TargetFilename:(*\\bw_setup.js OR *\\bw1.js OR */bw_setup.js OR */bw1.js) OR @CommandLine:(*bw_setup.js* OR *bw1.js*))
(#event_simpleName=FileWritten OR #event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 OR #event_simpleName=SyntheticProcessRollup2)
| (SHA256HashData=/^18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb$/i OR SHA256HashData=/^8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14$/i OR TargetFileName=/(bw_setup|bw1)\.js$/i OR CommandLine=/(bw_setup|bw1)\.js/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, TargetFileName, SHA256HashData, ImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb","8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14") OR Filesystem.file_name IN ("bw_setup.js","bw1.js") by host Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb","8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14") OR Filesystem.file_name IN ("bw_setup.js","bw1.js") by host Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

SecurityEvent

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb", "8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14") or SHA1 in~ ("18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb", "8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14") or MD5 in~ ("18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb", "8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb", "8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14") or SHA1 in~ ("18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb", "8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14") or MD5 in~ ("18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb", "8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["18f784b3bc9a0bcdcb1a8d7f51bc5f54323fc40cbd874119354ab609bef6e4cb", "8605e365edf11160aad517c7d79a3b26b62290e5072ef97b102a01ddbb343f14"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CanisterSprawl: pgserve Compromised on npm: Malicious Versions Harvest Credentials and Exfiltrate to a Decentralized ICP Canister

StepSecurity
2026-05-04 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On April 21, 2026, malicious versions of pgserve were published to npm. pgserve is an embedded PostgreSQL server for development — zero config, auto-provisioned databases, designed to be dropped into any Node.js project. The compromised versions (1.1.11, 1.1.12, and 1.1.13) inject a 1,143-line credential-harvesting script that runs via postinstall on every npm install.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-31431")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-31431")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

Mini Shai-Hulud: Python subprocess spawns `_runtime/start.py` from lightning site-packages AIInstallation High
Detects the malicious `__init__.py` bootstrap pattern in lightning 2.6.2/2.6.3 where a background thread spawns `start.py` from a `_runtime` subdirectory of the lightning package via `subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, _start], cwd=_runtime_dir, ...)`. The combination of Python parent + `_runtime` + `start.py` + lightning path is article-specific and not seen in benign workflows. Rationale: The malicious `__init__.py` snippet quoted verbatim in the article shows `subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, _start], cwd=_runtime_dir, ...)` where `_start = lightning/_runtime/start.py`. The three-way AND (python parent + `_runtime/start.py` + `lightning` path) is unique to this campaign and has no legitimate equivalent in the lightning project's actual source. Corroborated by Semgrep and Socket.dev write-ups of the same package. Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/malicious-dependency-in-pytorch-lightning-used-for-ai-training/ • https://socket.dev/supply-chain-attacks/mini-shai-hulud • https://insiderllm.com/guides/pytorch-lightning-malware-local-ai-audit/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1129

Mini Shai-Hulud PyPI payload known SHA256 (start.py / router_runtime.js) AIInstallation High
Hash-match alert for the two specific malicious files dropped inside the compromised lightning 2.6.2/2.6.3 package: `start.py` (Bun bootstrapper) and `router_runtime.js` (11 MB credential stealer). Triggers on file write, image load, or process execution observing either hash. Rationale: Pure IOC match on the two SHA256 hashes published directly in the article: `5f5852b5...` (router_runtime.js) and `8046a111...` (start.py). Hash collisions are not a concern at SHA256 strength, so any hit is the named malware. Hashes cross-validated by Semgrep's independent analysis of the same compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/malicious-dependency-in-pytorch-lightning-used-for-ai-training/ • https://socket.dev/supply-chain-attacks/mini-shai-hulud

Mini Shai-Hulud: Bun runtime executing `router_runtime.js` (2nd-stage stealer) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the second stage of the Mini Shai-Hulud attack: after start.py downloads Bun v1.3.13, it executes the 11 MB `router_runtime.js` payload that exfiltrates SSH keys, cloud creds, crypto wallets, and VPN secrets. Catching `bun` (or `bun.exe`) launching `router_runtime.js` is the most reliable behavioural marker shared with the prior Bitwarden CLI and SAP npm waves. Rationale: The article explicitly names `router_runtime.js` as the 11 MB Bun-executed payload reached via `start.py` downloading Bun v1.3.13. Wiz and Mend write-ups confirm the same `bun <stealer>.js` pattern reused across TanStack, Bitwarden CLI, and SAP waves of the same worm — generalising the filename set (`router_runtime.js`, `router_init.js`, `tanstack_runner.js`) catches the campaign without losing article-specificity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-tanstack-more-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.mend.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-172-npm-and-pypi-packages-compromised-in-latest-wave/ • https://socket.dev/supply-chain-attacks/mini-shai-hulud
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1552.001 T1555 T1041

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("router_runtime.js","router_init.js","tanstack_runner.js") or ProcessCommandLine has "_runtime" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("router_runtime.js","router_init.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("router_runtime.js","router_init.js","tanstack_runner.js") or TargetProcessCommandLine has "_runtime"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2") or SHA1 in~ ("5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2") or MD5 in~ ("5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2") or SHA1 in~ ("5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2") or MD5 in~ ("5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

lightning PyPI Compromise: A Bun-Based Credential Stealer in Python

Snyk
2026-04-30 11 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious release of the lightning PyPI package ships a credential-stealing Bun payload that runs on import. Snyk has a live advisory. Here's what's in the package, what to rotate, and how the payload pattern connects to the Mini Shai-Hulud npm campaign one day earlier.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — lightning PyPI Compromise: A Bun-Based Credential Stealer in Python
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] lightning PyPI compromise artifacts: start.py / router_runtime.js write · [LLM] Python child process executing lightning _runtime/start.py bootstrapper · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud style repository poisoning — .claude/router_runtime.js drop · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
lightning PyPI compromise artifacts: start.py / router_runtime.js write AIInstallation Medium
Detects file write of the two malicious payloads dropped inside the lightning 2.6.2/2.6.3 wheel — by SHA256 hash or by the canonical hidden _runtime path. Hash-pinned alerting on a confirmed supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Anchors on the three SHA256 hashes Snyk published in the advisory (start.py 8046a1..., router_runtime.js 5f5852..., wheel 56070a...) with a path-pattern backup for the _runtime directory canonical to this attack. Cross-checked Snyk advisory SNYK-PYTHON-LIGHTNING-16323121, StepSecurity write-up, Socket research blog, and BleepingComputer reporting — all three vendors cite the same hashes and the _runtime/start.py + _runtime/router_runtime.js drop pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/lightning-pypi-compromise-bun-based-credential-stealer/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/lightning-obfuscated-javascript-credential-stealer-bundled-in-pypi-wheel • https://socket.dev/blog/lightning-pypi-package-compromised • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/backdoored-pytorch-lightning-package-drops-credential-stealer/ • https://safedep.io/malicious-pytorch-lightning-pypi-compromise/

Python child process executing lightning _runtime/start.py bootstrapper AIInstallation High
Detects the Python subprocess spawn pattern wired into the malicious lightning __init__.py: `subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '<...>/lightning/_runtime/start.py'], cwd='<...>/_runtime')`. Fires whenever any Python interpreter launches the Bun downloader as a child. Rationale: Anchored on the unique cmdline shape produced by the malicious lightning __init__.py's `subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '<...>/lightning/_runtime/start.py'], cwd='<...>/_runtime')`. The path token `lightning/_runtime/start.py` does not occur in clean lightning 2.6.1 or in pytorch-lightning (which is unaffected). Cross-checked against Snyk advisory and pydevtools deep-dive, which both reproduce the __init__.py snippet verbatim. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/lightning-pypi-compromise-bun-based-credential-stealer/ • https://pydevtools.com/blog/lightning-pypi-compromise-import-time-supply-chain-attack/ • https://socket.dev/blog/lightning-pypi-package-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1105

| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","python3.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)lightning[\\/]_runtime[\\/]start\.py"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3","python")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)lightning[\\/]_runtime[\\/]start\.py"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud style repository poisoning — .claude/router_runtime.js drop AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the post-compromise artifacts the lightning stealer commits into developer repositories via GitHub GraphQL createCommitOnBranch (masked as 'claude' Anthropic Claude Code activity): .claude/router_runtime.js, .claude/setup.mjs, .vscode/setup.mjs, .github/workflows/format-check.yml. Rationale: The article enumerates the exact file set the GraphQL `createCommitOnBranch` mutation drops into victim repos (`.claude/router_runtime.js`, `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/setup.mjs`, `.vscode/tasks.json`, `.vscode/setup.mjs`, `.github/workflows/format-check.yml`). I excluded `.vscode/tasks.json` (high FP — legitimate VS Code file) and `.claude/settings.json` (common with real Claude Code adoption) and kept the high-fidelity `router_runtime.js` + `setup.mjs` + `format-check.yml` triplet. Snyk, Socket, and safedep all corroborate the same file-drop list as the post-compromise repo poisoning behaviour shared with the Mini Shai-Hulud npm wave. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/lightning-pypi-compromise-bun-based-credential-stealer/ • https://socket.dev/blog/lightning-pypi-package-compromised • https://safedep.io/malicious-pytorch-lightning-pypi-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/lightning-obfuscated-javascript-credential-stealer-bundled-in-pypi-wheel

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.

DeviceProcessEvents

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2", "5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "56070a9d8de0c0ffb1ec5c309953cf4679432df5a78df9aeb020fbb73d2be9fb", "f1b3e7b3eec3294c4d6b5f87854a52471f03997f", "40d0f21b64ec8fb3a7a1959897252e09") or SHA1 in~ ("8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2", "5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "56070a9d8de0c0ffb1ec5c309953cf4679432df5a78df9aeb020fbb73d2be9fb", "f1b3e7b3eec3294c4d6b5f87854a52471f03997f", "40d0f21b64ec8fb3a7a1959897252e09") or MD5 in~ ("8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2", "5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "56070a9d8de0c0ffb1ec5c309953cf4679432df5a78df9aeb020fbb73d2be9fb", "f1b3e7b3eec3294c4d6b5f87854a52471f03997f", "40d0f21b64ec8fb3a7a1959897252e09")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2", "5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "56070a9d8de0c0ffb1ec5c309953cf4679432df5a78df9aeb020fbb73d2be9fb", "f1b3e7b3eec3294c4d6b5f87854a52471f03997f", "40d0f21b64ec8fb3a7a1959897252e09") or SHA1 in~ ("8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2", "5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "56070a9d8de0c0ffb1ec5c309953cf4679432df5a78df9aeb020fbb73d2be9fb", "f1b3e7b3eec3294c4d6b5f87854a52471f03997f", "40d0f21b64ec8fb3a7a1959897252e09") or MD5 in~ ("8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2", "5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "56070a9d8de0c0ffb1ec5c309953cf4679432df5a78df9aeb020fbb73d2be9fb", "f1b3e7b3eec3294c4d6b5f87854a52471f03997f", "40d0f21b64ec8fb3a7a1959897252e09")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["8046a11187c135da6959862ff3846e99ad15462d2ec8a2f77a30ad53ebd5dcf2", "5f5852b5f604369945118937b058e49064612ac69826e0adadca39a357dfb5b1", "56070a9d8de0c0ffb1ec5c309953cf4679432df5a78df9aeb020fbb73d2be9fb", "f1b3e7b3eec3294c4d6b5f87854a52471f03997f", "40d0f21b64ec8fb3a7a1959897252e09"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — lightning PyPI Compromise: A Bun-Based Credential Stealer in Python Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — lightning PyPI Compromise: A Bun-Based Credential Stealer in Python
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("start.py", "router_runtime.js", "__init__.py", "execution.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("start.py", "router_runtime.js", "__init__.py", "execution.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine

npm preinstall hook executes 'node setup.mjs' / 'bun execution.js' (Mini Shai-Hulud SAP supply chain) AIInstallation High
Detects the two-stage process chain unique to the Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm: a node.exe invocation of the malicious preinstall bootstrapper setup.mjs, and the downloaded Bun runtime executing the obfuscated execution.js payload. This is the deterministic on-host signature of the @cap-js/sqlite, @cap-js/postgres, @cap-js/db-service, and mbt package compromises. Rationale: setup.mjs and execution.js are the two file names hard-coded into the malware (article: 'The malicious package adds two files: setup.mjs, execution.js'). The two-arm OR catches both the npm-install bootstrap stage and the Bun-runtime second stage. No legitimate npm package ships a script literally named execution.js executed under Bun. Cross-checked against Sophos and Wiz write-ups confirming identical file names and process chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack-targets-sap-npm-packages • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm • https://onapsis.com/blog/sap-cap-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.mend.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-172-npm-and-pypi-packages-compromised-in-latest-wave/

    or (FileName has_any ("bun","bun.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "execution.js")
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688

  )

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mini Shai-Hulud 'OhNoWhatsGoingOnWithGitHub' dead-drop keyword in outbound URL AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the unique propagation keyword 'OhNoWhatsGoingOnWithGitHub' appearing in outbound HTTP/HTTPS URLs, web-proxy logs, or process telemetry. The malware queries https://api.github.com/search/commits?q=OhNoWhatsGoingOnWithGitHub to harvest base64-encoded GitHub tokens left in commit messages as a dead-drop. The string has no legitimate use anywhere. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'OhNoWhatsGoingOnWithGitHub' as the propagation keyword / GitHub commit dead-drop marker and gives the exact API endpoint: https://api.github.com/search/commits?q=OhNoWhatsGoingOnWithGitHub. This string is unique to the campaign - any occurrence in URL, command-line, or proxy log is a high-fidelity hit. Cross-checked against Wiz and Sophos blogs which independently cite the same keyword. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack-targets-sap-npm-packages • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm • https://safedep.io/mini-shai-hulud-and-sap-compromise/ • https://phoenix.security/mini-shai-hulud-sap-cap-mbt-npm-supply-chain-bun-credential-stealer/

Mini Shai-Hulud known SHA256 IOC match (setup.mjs / execution.js / runner-memory dumper) AIInstallation Medium
Sweeps endpoint file-event and process telemetry for the three SHA256 hashes published in the Mini Shai-Hulud sample analysis: the setup.mjs Bun bootstrapper, the 11.7 MB execution.js credential-stealer, and the embedded Python /proc Runner.Worker memory dumper. A single hit confirms the compromised package was unpacked or executed on the host. Rationale: Article publishes three SHA256 hashes from the analyzed @cap-js/sqlite@2.2.2 sample under Indicators of Compromise. Hash matches are by definition zero-FP for these specific files. Sweeps file-create, process-execute, and image-load tables to catch the payload regardless of how it landed on disk. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack-targets-sap-npm-packages • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm • https://onapsis.com/blog/sap-cap-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes

]);
union
  ( DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 in (bad_hashes)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              Actor=InitiatingProcessAccountName,

              EventClass="FileEvent" ),
  ( DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 in (bad_hashes)
       or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (bad_hashes)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Actor=AccountName,
              FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              EventClass="ProcessEvent" ),
  ( DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 in (bad_hashes)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Actor=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine="",
              EventClass="ImageLoad" )
| order by Timestamp desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high

        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Malicious tanstack npm postinstall hook executing postinstall.cjs AIInstallation High
Detects the postinstall hook from the hijacked unscoped 'tanstack' npm package (versions 2.0.4-2.0.7) executing during 'npm install' or 'npm ci'. The npm process spawns node.exe to run node_modules/tanstack/postinstall.cjs which reads .env files and POSTs them to a Svix Ingest webhook. Rationale: Article specifies postinstall.cjs is the dropped payload inside node_modules/tanstack/ and that npm install triggers it. The node.exe-under-npm parent chain plus the exact relative path 'tanstack/postinstall.cjs' is article-specific and unlikely to fire on legitimate packages.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately installs an unrelated package whose folder contains the literal string 'tanstack' (very low — string match is path-anchored)
  • Internal forks/mirrors of the real @tanstack/* scoped packages relocated to an unscoped 'tanstack' folder during build tooling
  • Security researcher detonating the IOC in a sandbox connected to corporate telemetry
  • CI runner replaying historical lockfiles that still pin tanstack@2.0.x prior to remediation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@tanstack/","@tanstack\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent npm command — confirm the package version against the IOC list (2.0.4-2.0.7) by reading node_modules/tanstack/package.json on the host. Capture user, repo path, and CI job ID. 2) Contain: isolate the developer endpoint or the CI runner, revoke all secrets that lived in .env files in that working directory at install time (AWS keys, GitHub PATs, npm publish tokens, OpenAI/Anthropic keys, DB strings). Pin lockfiles away from tanstack unscoped. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound traffic to api.svix.com within ±5 min of the install, search all repos in the org for 'tanstack' (unscoped) in package.json / package-lock.json / yarn.lock / pnpm-lock.yaml, and review CloudTrail/GitHub audit logs for anomalous use of any leaked credentials.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")

Svix Ingest webhook exfiltration relay (src_3387PLMB2uhXOBe3Q8sHu) AIexfiltration High
Detects outbound HTTPS POST traffic to the attacker-controlled Svix Ingest source ID used by the tanstack package to relay stolen .env contents. Hits should be extremely rare in a development pipeline that doesn't legitimately use this Svix tenant. Rationale: src_3387PLMB2uhXOBe3Q8sHu and the ingest token 3j2jokvbaF4WWdngv8zBbk are unique strings from the article's payload URL. api.svix.com is a trusted SaaS so the source ID is what makes this high-fidelity rather than naive domain blocking.
ATT&CKT1567 T1102.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineering team legitimately uses Svix Ingest for product webhooks — but those would use a different src_ ID
  • Security tooling actively probing the IOC URL for verification
  • Sandbox detonations of the package in lab environments
  • Threat-intel feed integrations resolving api.svix.com for IOC enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm POST direction and payload size to the URL; identify whether the initiating process is node.exe under an npm install context. Capture the user and host. 2) Contain: block the specific Svix source ID at the proxy/firewall (keep api.svix.com itself open if other teams rely on Svix), revoke all secrets that could have been in .env at the install location. 3) Hunt: look back 90 days for any other host reaching the same src_ ID, sweep the org for tanstack package presence in lockfiles, and check the user's GitHub/AWS/npm activity for anomalous post-install actions.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.svix.com"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("src_3387PLMB2uhXOBe3Q8sHu","3j2jokvbaF4WWdngv8zBbk","/ingest/api/v1/source/")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Url has "api.svix.com" and Url has_any ("src_3387PLMB2uhXOBe3Q8sHu","3j2jokvbaF4WWdngv8zBbk","/ingest/api/v1/source/")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, EventProduct),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery =~ "api.svix.com" or DnsQuery has "svix.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, EventProduct),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where RequestURL has "api.svix.com" and RequestURL has_any ("src_3387PLMB2uhXOBe3Q8sHu","3j2jokvbaF4WWdngv8zBbk","/ingest/api/v1/source/")
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js postinstall reading .env / .env.* during package install AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the file-access pattern of the tanstack 2.0.6 directory sweep where node.exe (spawned by npm install) reads .env, .env.local, .env.production, .env.staging, .env.development from the project root within seconds of package extraction. Rationale: Article details exact filename targets in 2.0.4/2.0.5/2.0.7 (.env + .env.local) and the directory-sweep in 2.0.6 that catches .env / .env.local / .env.production / .env.staging / .env.development. Threshold of >=2 distinct env files read by a single node.exe instance is the high-fidelity behavioural signal.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • dotenv / dotenv-cli legitimate library loading multiple .env files at app start
  • Build tooling like Vite/Next.js/Nuxt reading several .env.<mode> files during build
  • Test runners that switch between .env.test and .env.development
  • CI environment-variable injection scripts copying .env files between locations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("vite","next build","next start","nuxt","jest","vitest","webpack","rollup") and not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of the node.exe instance is an npm install/ci process tree (not a long-running app server). Inspect the working directory — if a tanstack folder exists under node_modules, treat as confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: isolate the host, rotate all credentials present in any .env file at the working-directory location, kill any in-flight CI jobs that ran the tanstack install. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host where node.exe under npm has read .env files in the last 60 days, cross-reference with the Svix detection (UC2), and confirm whether stolen credentials are being used externally via CloudTrail/GitHub audit logs.
let envFiles = dynamic([".env",".env.local",".env.production",".env.staging",".env.development",".env.test"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRead","FileAccessed")
   or isnotempty(FileName)
| where FileName in~ (envFiles) or FileName startswith ".env."
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), EnvFilesRead=make_set(FileName), FolderPaths=make_set(FolderPath), CmdLine=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where array_length(EnvFilesRead) >= 2 or (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm") and array_length(EnvFilesRead) >= 1)
| order by FirstSeen desc
let envFiles = dynamic([".env",".env.local",".env.production",".env.staging",".env.development",".env.test"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","/node","\\node")
| where TargetFileName in~ (envFiles) or TargetFileName startswith ".env."
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), EnvFilesRead=make_set(TargetFileName), FolderPaths=make_set(TargetFilePath), CmdLine=any(ActingProcessCommandLine)
    by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where array_length(EnvFilesRead) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd) (@Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */bin/node)) (@TargetFilename:(*\\.env OR *\\.env.local OR *\\.env.production OR *\\.env.staging OR *\\.env.development) OR @file.path:(*/.env OR */.env.local OR */.env.production OR */.env.staging OR */.env.development))
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i OR ContextImageFileName=/\/node$/i
| regex("[\\\\/](\\.env(\\.[a-z]+)?)$", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| count >= 2

Known-bad tanstack 2.0.4-2.0.7 package tarball SHA256 file hash on disk AIDelivery Medium
Direct hash-based hit on the SHA256 IOCs published for the malicious tanstack@2.0.4-2.0.7 packages. Fires when an endpoint writes or executes a file matching one of the published hashes, anchoring the campaign to a specific host. Rationale: Direct SHA256 IOC hit is the highest-fidelity detection available — the article publishes four hashes for the malicious tanstack tarballs (2.0.4-2.0.7). Hash collisions are effectively impossible, so any positive is a confirmed compromise.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox detonating the IOC on managed analyst VMs
  • Security researcher reproducing the attack chain
  • Malware-analysis VMs where the package was intentionally installed for study
  • No legitimate FP scenario exists for the production fleet
Response runbook
1) Triage: immediately confirm the file path — node_modules/tanstack/* under a real project tree is a confirmed compromise; an isolated sample under an analyst path is benign. Pull the host's npm install logs and git history for any commits touching package.json/lockfiles. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate any node.exe instances spawned from the affected node_modules, force-rotate every credential the user/CI could have accessed, and pull lockfiles back to a known-good baseline. 3) Hunt: pivot org-wide on all four SHA256s, look for outbound traffic to api.svix.com from the same hosts (UC2), and audit downstream supply-chain: any package these developers published in the same window may itself be compromised.
let badHashes = dynamic(["72ec4571e27c06f1d48737477c2b38a4f90d699950dab8946b48591133dc4f90","04ee5325c8900c9d644ed81c9012525b6fc19f21c65cef85b6ba98b6a0a23566","abc164807947b102164488a08161adb4ee08be6b78a371350a6b156eed0d97d9","7bb84e6ba893248814cd3bac70b7bdc115740fba9e13419940c73460cbcd7b6f"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | where SHA256 in (badHashes)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | where SHA256 in (badHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (badHashes)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let badHashes = dynamic(["72ec4571e27c06f1d48737477c2b38a4f90d699950dab8946b48591133dc4f90","04ee5325c8900c9d644ed81c9012525b6fc19f21c65cef85b6ba98b6a0a23566","abc164807947b102164488a08161adb4ee08be6b78a371350a6b156eed0d97d9","7bb84e6ba893248814cd3bac70b7bdc115740fba9e13419940c73460cbcd7b6f"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
    | where TargetFileSHA256 in (badHashes) or Hash in (badHashes)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
    | where SHA256 in (badHashes)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
